rationale_shown_to_reviewer: The prediction and inference objectives are framed around estimating and interpreting f or f-hat, so understanding statistical learning as estimating an unknown predictor-response function is needed for stable understanding of the distinction.
Reducible error is defined as error from imperfect estimation of f and irreducible error as variation not captured by X, so the unknown-function framing is foundational for the error decomposition.
Parametric and non-parametric methods are alternative approaches to estimating f, distinguished by whether they assume an explicit functional form for that unknown function.

The prediction-versus-inference distinction explains why accuracy-focused settings may tolerate black-box flexibility while inference-focused settings require interpretability of predictor-response relationships.
The contrast between restrictive parametric assumptions and more flexible non-parametric fitting provides concrete method classes for understanding flexibility and interpretability trade-offs.
Understanding prediction as accurate estimation of unknown responses explains why test MSE on unseen observations is the relevant performance target rather than training MSE alone.
Overfitting is defined by the divergence between low training error and worse test performance, so distinguishing training MSE from test MSE is necessary to understand it stably.
The bias-variance trade-off decomposes expected test MSE into variance, squared bias, and irreducible error, so understanding reducible versus irreducible error is foundational.
Model flexibility helps explain overfitting because excessively flexible methods can fit noise or chance patterns in the training data and fail to generalize.
The bias-variance trade-off depends on how model flexibility tends to reduce bias while increasing variance, so the concept of flexibility is needed for stable understanding.
The bias-variance trade-off is stated in terms of expected test MSE and good test performance, so understanding test MSE is required for the target concept.

The bias-variance trade-off explains why highly flexible methods can have increased variance and poor test performance despite fitting training data closely, which strengthens the explanation of overfitting.
Simple linear regression assumes a linear functional form with finitely many coefficients, making the parametric-method framework explanatory for its modeling structure.
Least squares fitting in this context chooses the intercept and slope for the simple linear regression line, so the model structure must be understood before the fitting criterion.

Multiple linear regression extends the linear-regression slope-and-intercept framework from one predictor to several predictors, making the simple model a cognitive prerequisite for interpreting multiple-regression coefficients.
Residual standard error and R-squared are based on residual variation and RSS, so understanding residuals and residual sum of squares is needed to understand these fit measures.
Regression confidence intervals use standard errors to quantify uncertainty in coefficient or mean-response estimates, making coefficient-estimate uncertainty foundational to interval interpretation.
The distinction between reducible estimation uncertainty and irreducible individual-response variation explains why prediction intervals are wider than confidence intervals.
Regression coefficient t-tests use coefficient estimates relative to their standard errors, so understanding standard errors is necessary for stable interpretation of these tests.

Interaction effects alter how a predictor's association or slope depends on another predictor, so understanding coefficient interpretation in multi-predictor regression is needed to interpret interactions stably.
Polynomial regression illustrates how adding transformed predictor terms increases the range of shapes a model can represent while preserving a linear-coefficient framework.
A central consequence of collinearity is inflated coefficient standard errors, so understanding standard errors is required to understand how collinearity increases coefficient uncertainty.

Collinearity concerns difficulty separating individual predictor effects in multiple regression, which depends on understanding coefficients as conditional associations holding other predictors fixed.
Collinearity explains why inflated standard errors can weaken t-statistics and make coefficient-level association tests harder to interpret.
Residual diagnostics interpret residuals produced by a fitted least-squares regression, so understanding residuals and the fitted model is required first.
A curved residual pattern supplies diagnostic motivation for adding transformed predictor terms to represent non-linear relationships.
Checking regression error assumptions supports responsible interpretation of interval estimates whose validity depends on the fitted model and error structure.
Outlier and influence diagnostics depend on fitted values and residuals from the regression fit, making least-squares residual understanding foundational.
Residual plots and studentized residuals provide direct evidence for possible outliers, while related leverage checks distinguish unusual predictor configurations.
Dummy-variable coefficients are interpreted as conditional group differences relative to a baseline, building on multiple-regression coefficient interpretation.
